topic: Scoped onchain delegation on BNB Smart Chain (chain 56): the cryptographic enforcement layer — EIP-7702, ERC-4337, ERC-7579 SmartSessions, ERC-7710/7715
executive_summary:
Bottom line: AiKi can make the statement "this agent may call Venus.repayBorrow with at most 250 USDT, revocable instantly" and have it be CHAIN-ENFORCED on BSC today, with no backend in the trust path. The "over a rolling 30 days" clause cannot — no shipping module implements a time-windowed cumulative cap.

Verified by direct RPC against chain 56 (not by blog): (1) EIP-7702 is live. Pascal hardfork, timestamp 1742436600 = 2025-03-20 02:10:00 UTC per bnb-chain/bsc params/config.go. A 60-block scan at head 116,725,156 found 49 of 3,492 txs with type 0x4 (1.40%), each carrying an authorizationList with chainId 0x38. Your ~1.5% measurement is confirmed; anvil's "Eip7702 is not supported" is an anvil limitation, not a BSC one. (2) All three EntryPoints are deployed and answering getNonce on BSC: v0.6 0x5FF137D4…2789, v0.7 0x0000000071727De2…a032, v0.8 0x4337084D9E255Ff0…f108. One observed type-4 tx targets EntryPoint v0.8 directly — the 7702+4337-v0.8 combined path is live in production on BSC. (3) Rhinestone SmartSession (0x00000000008bDABA73cD9815d79069c247Eb4bDA) is deployed on BSC and returns isModuleType(1)==true. SpendingLimitsPolicy, UniversalActionPolicy and SudoPolicy are deployed. TimeFramePolicy, UsageLimitPolicy and ValueLimitPolicy are NOT deployed at their canonical addresses on 56 — they return 0x. You must deploy them.

The hard constraint: I read ERC20SpendingLimitPolicy.sol. It stores `alreadySpent` as a monotonic counter against a fixed `spendingLimit`, contains no block.timestamp, and never resets. It is a lifetime cap on a session, not a rolling window. "250 USDT per 30 days, renewing" requires a custom policy contract.

Weakest area of this report: I did not verify any bundler or paymaster actually serving chain 56 against primary docs, nor Biconomy/Safe/thirdweb/Alchemy BSC support. Treat those as unresearched.

findings.claim: EIP-7702 is live on BSC mainnet via the Pascal hardfork, activated at unix timestamp 1742436600 = 2025-03-20 02:10:00 UTC. CONFIRMED, both by client source and by live type-4 traffic.
findings.detail: DEPLOYED + SPEC. bnb-chain/bsc params/config.go BSCChainConfig gives PascalTime = 1742436600 with the inline comment "2025-03-20 02:10:00 AM UTC". BSC is timestamp-forked, not block-forked, so there is no fork block number. The official BNB Chain announcement names EIP-7702 explicitly as a Pascal goal (it separately names BEP-439/EIP-2537 for BLS12-381; I did not find a BEP number specifically covering 7702 — that is a gap). Later BSC forks in the same file: Lorentz 1745903100, Maxwell 1751250600, Fermi 1768357800, Osaka 1777343400, Mendel 1777343400, Pasteur 1787625000 (2026-08-25, i.e. next week). Live confirmation: scanning 60 consecutive blocks at head 116,725,156 on bsc-dataseed.bnbchain.org yielded 3,492 txs of which 49 (1.40%) had type == "0x4" and a populated authorizationList with chainId 0x38. Your ~1.5% measurement reproduces. The anvil failure "Eip7702 is not supported" is anvil's hardfork config lagging, not a chain property.

findings.detail:

- 0x22a9d0f7e023bcc4d907f5142fac4d44e87dccb62b33b3e6614ab885e50fc2ed, block 116725154, from 0xb849f1de…1056, to 0xc038adf6…921e, authorization delegating to 0x10debea5bcf59ed26692bb99a8ab8452d594112d, auth nonce 0x0.
- 0xa735cf7917e8d8b03f3123304ff5274af4e430c90dd8c93544adb3d3e2689bed, block 116725153, to 0x4337084d9e255ff0702461cf8895ce9e3b5ff108 (EntryPoint v0.8), delegate 0x6c35fbcf24e57e5aa2e3aa2ca82e052499d02cf8, auth nonce 0x9f.
- 0xf10f780f27fa198fdcb21f663d834a77a0a07343a839ea9b4bf0565d8f33b446, block 116725152, self-send from/to 0x42027f35…c0a1, same delegate 0x6c35fbcf…2cf8, auth nonce 0x10a.
Most-used delegate implementations across the 60-block window (with code length in hex chars from eth_getCode): 0x2c80d90a70a64108dbc2d6babce1cd749dfbc841 (16 auths, 41686), 0x8e377abe448ec9f8ed9d00553676ee2855739a9b (16, 46576), 0x8ab3e5db1d29918b38339ff18c2dd32f6f0ceae3 (7, 1580), 0xb1280932da6df283be6dddd99f2a147d41773988 (4, 1580), 0x6c35fbcf24e57e5aa2e3aa2ca82e052499d02cf8. I could not identify these implementations by project name — gap.

findings.claim: All three canonical ERC-4337 EntryPoints (v0.6, v0.7, v0.8) are deployed on BSC chain 56 and functionally respond.
findings.detail: DEPLOYED. eth_getCode returned non-empty for: v0.6 0x5FF137D4b0FDCD49DcA30c7CF57E578a026d2789 (47380 hex chars), v0.7 0x0000000071727De22E5E9d8BAf0edAc6f37da032 (32072), v0.8 0x4337084D9E255Ff0702461CF8895CE9E3b5Ff108 (43478). SimpleAccountFactory v0.6 0x9406Cc6185a346906296840746125a0E44976454 is also deployed (6478). Functional probe: eth_call of getNonce(address,uint192) selector 0x35567e1a with key=0x2a returned 0x…002a<<64 on all three, i.e. the correct EntryPoint nonce packing (key in the high 192 bits, sequence 0) — this is behavioural confirmation, not just bytecode presence. Chain id confirmed 0x38. These are the same deterministic CREATE2 addresses used on every EVM chain, so cross-chain tooling addresses will work unmodified on 56.

findings.claim: Rhinestone SmartSession (ERC-7579 session-key validator) IS deployed on BSC chain 56 — but only 5 of 8 policy modules are. TimeFramePolicy, UsageLimitPolicy and ValueLimitPolicy return empty code on 56.
findings.detail:
DEPLOYED. Addresses taken verbatim from rhinestonewtf/module-sdk src/module/smart-sessions/**/constants.ts, then eth_getCode against chain 56 (hex-string length, 2 = empty):
- SmartSession 0x00000000008bDABA73cD9815d79069c247Eb4bDA → 47218 ✅. Behavioural proof: isModuleType(1) (selector 0xecd05961) returns 1, i.e. it self-reports as an ERC-7579 VALIDATOR. isInitialized(0x11…11) returns 0.
- SmartSessionCompatibilityFallback 0x000000000052e9685932845660777DF43C2dC496 → 4880 ✅
- SpendingLimitsPolicy 0x00000088D48cF102A8Cdb0137A9b173f957c6343 → 6234 ✅ (supportsInterface(0x01ffc9a7)==true)
- UniversalActionPolicy 0x0000006DDA6c463511C4e9B05CFc34C1247fCF1F → 6170 ✅ (ERC165 true)
- SudoPolicy 0x0000003111cD8e92337C100F22B7A9dbf8DEE301 → 2298 ✅
- TimeFramePolicy 0x8177451511dE0577b911C254E9551D981C26dc72 → EMPTY ❌
- UsageLimitPolicy 0x1F34eF8311345A3A4a4566aF321b313052F51493 → EMPTY ❌
- ValueLimitPolicy 0x730DA93267E7E513e932301B47F2ac7D062abC83 → EMPTY ❌
So expiry, call-count caps and native-BNB value caps have no live enforcement contract on BSC today. They are permissionless CREATE2 deploys you can push yourself from the audited source.

findings.claim: THE HARD ONE: no shipping module enforces a cumulative spend cap over a rolling time window. ERC20SpendingLimitPolicy is a LIFETIME cap with no timestamp logic and no reset.
findings.detail: SPEC, read from source. contracts/external/policies/ERC20SpendingLimitPolicy.sol (260 lines): struct TokenPolicyData { uint256 alreadySpent; … uint256 spendingLimit; } keyed by mapping(ConfigId => mapping(address multiplexer => mapping(address token => mapping(address userOpSender => TokenPolicyData)))). checkAction() does `newData.alreadySpent += amount; totalSpentAndApproved = newData.alreadySpent + newData.approvedAmount; if (totalSpentAndApproved > newData.spendingLimit) …` then persists `$.alreadySpent`. Grepping for block.timestamp in this file returns NOTHING. alreadySpent is monotonic; the only reset is at re-initialisation (`$.spendingLimit = 0; $.alreadySpent = 0;` in the deinit path). Same for UsageLimitPolicy (uint128 limit/used, no timestamp) and ValueLimitPolicy (valueLimit/limitUsed, no timestamp). TimeFramePolicy is the ONLY time-aware policy and it only does `block.timestamp < validUntil && block.timestamp >= validAfter` — an absolute window, not a renewing one. Conclusion: a renewing 30-day allowance requires a custom IActionPolicy. Writing one is ~100 lines (store windowStart + spentInWindow; if block.timestamp >= windowStart + period, reset). Note it must be storage-writing in validation, which has ERC-4337 storage-access implications for bundler acceptance.

findings.claim: The spending-limit policy counts ERC-20 approvals against the cap, not just transfers. This matters enormously for a Venus.repayBorrow flow.
findings.detail: SPEC, from source. ERC20SpendingLimitPolicy tracks both `alreadySpent` and `approvedAmount`, and the check is `alreadySpent + approvedAmount > spendingLimit`. The source contains branches decoding approve / transfer / transferFrom calldata, with comments about approvals to the account itself reverting in the token contract. Architectural consequence for AiKi: Venus.repayBorrow(underlying) pulls tokens via transferFrom, so the account must first approve Venus. That approve() call is the thing the SpendingLimitsPolicy actually caps — the policy is an ERC-20-calldata-aware ACTION policy that must be bound to the USDT token address as target, not to Venus. Capping the Venus call itself (argument-level: repayBorrow's uint256 amount) is the job of UniversalActionPolicy / ArgPolicy, which inspect calldata arguments against rules. I did not read UniActionPolicy.sol or ArgPolicy.sol, so treat the exact rule encoding as unverified.

findings.claim: SmartSessions has five audit reports in-repo, including two 2026 Cantina reports — one specifically covering the external policies.
findings.detail: Repo file listing via GitHub trees API: audits/[ChainLight] Rhinestone SmartSessions Security Audit v1.0.pdf; audits/report-cantinacode-rhinestone-0826-core.pdf; audits/report-cantinacode-rhinestone-0826-external-policies.pdf; audits/rhinestone_smartsessions_update.pdf; audits/rhinestone_smartsessions_v1.pdf. The "0826" naming suggests August 2026 engagements — i.e. current. I did NOT open the PDFs, so I cannot state findings, severity counts, or whether issues were remediated. The existence of a dedicated external-policies audit is the relevant signal: the policy contracts (where your spend caps live) were reviewed separately from the core session manager. Full policy set shipped in-repo: ArgPolicy (+ArgPolicyTreeLib), ContractWhitelistPolicy, ERC20SpendingLimitPolicy, SimpleGasPolicy, SudoPolicy, TimeFramePolicy, UniActionPolicy, UsageLimitPolicy, ValueLimitPolicy. Core: SmartSession.sol, ISmartSession.sol, DataTypes.sol, SmartSessionCompatibilityFallback.sol.

findings.claim: ERC-7715 is still Draft. The RPC method is `wallet_requestExecutionPermissions` — NOT the `wallet_grantPermissions` name that older material uses. It hard-depends on ERC-7710.
findings.detail: SPEC. eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-7715: status Draft, Standards Track: ERC. Defines `wallet_requestExecutionPermissions` for a dApp to ask a wallet to grant execution permission on the user's behalf. Permission shape is a BasePermission { type: string, isAdjustmentAllowed: boolean, data: type-specific }, and the EIP explicitly declines to mandate an exhaustive permission-type list ("we expect more rule and permission types to be developed as wallets get more advanced"). ERC-7710 is a required dependency: the response must carry a `delegationManager` address, and redemption happens through ERC-7710's interfaces. Practical read for AiKi: 7715 is a REQUEST protocol, not an enforcement mechanism. Whether the granted permission is chain-enforced depends entirely on what the named delegationManager contract does — and the permission-type taxonomy being open-ended means two wallets can grant nominally-identical permissions with different enforcement. Do not treat a 7715 grant as a security guarantee without inspecting the delegationManager onchain.

findings.claim: ZeroDev officially lists BNB Smart Chain (56) under "Regular EVM Networks".
findings.detail: MARKETING/DOCS (vendor docs, not an onchain probe). docs.zerodev.app/sdk/faqs/chains lists "Binance Smart Chain | 56". The page does not state which EntryPoint or Kernel versions apply on that chain, so I cannot tell you whether Kernel v3 (ERC-7579-compatible) or only older Kernel is available on 56, nor whether ZeroDev's own permissions/session-key validators are deployed there. ZeroDev's material describes Kernel as an ERC-4337/ERC-7579 modular account with pluggable validators (passkeys, ECDSA, session keys, multisig) and a plugin framework. I did NOT verify any ZeroDev/Kernel contract address on chain 56 by eth_getCode — do that before relying on it. Note also that ZeroDev's own bundler serving 56 is a separate question from the SDK listing the chain.

findings.claim: Ranking by REAL security — what the chain enforces vs what a service promises.
findings.detail:
TIER 1, fully chain-enforced, available on BSC today: ERC-7579 SmartSession at 0x00000000008bDABA73cD9815d79069c247Eb4bDA with SpendingLimitsPolicy + UniversalActionPolicy + SudoPolicy. Every constraint is checked inside validation by deployed bytecode; no offchain party can be bribed or compromised into exceeding it. Revocation is an onchain state write by the account owner.
TIER 1b, identical enforcement, different account model: EIP-7702 delegate an existing BSC EOA to a 7579 account implementation, then install SmartSession. Same guarantees, EOA keeps its address. Extra revocation lever: re-sign an authorization to address(0) or to a new implementation — this nukes ALL delegated permissions atomically, and 7702 auth nonces mean an old authorization cannot be replayed.
TIER 2, chain-enforced but you own the code: a bespoke IValidator/IActionPolicy you write and audit — the only route to a rolling-window spend cap.
TIER 3, partially chain-enforced: plain ERC-20 approve(spender, 250e18). The 250 cap IS cryptographic. But there is no target allowlist beyond the single spender, no function-selector scoping, no expiry, and revocation is a second approve(0) tx. Insufficient for "may call Venus.repayBorrow".
TIER 4, NOT chain-enforced: any design where a backend co-signs, holds a 2-of-2 share, rate-limits, or simulates-then-signs. The user's money is protected by your uptime and your key hygiene, not by BSC. If AiKi ships this, the honest UI string is "AiKi will not let this agent exceed 250 USDT", never "the chain will not let it".

findings.claim: Constraint-by-constraint verdict for what can be encoded onchain in a BSC session key TODAY.
findings.detail:
Target allowlist — YES, chain-enforced. SmartSession binds policies per ActionId; ContractWhitelistPolicy exists in-repo (not verified deployed on 56). UniversalActionPolicy IS deployed on 56.
Function-selector allowlist — YES, chain-enforced, via the action/ActionId mechanism. I saw ERC20SpendingLimitPolicy.checkAction receive `target` and emit TokenSpent(id, msg.sender, target, account, amount, remaining), confirming action policies see the call target. Exact selector-binding encoding UNVERIFIED (did not read DataTypes.sol).
Per-call native value cap — module EXISTS (ValueLimitPolicy) but NOT DEPLOYED on 56. Deploy it. Note it is a cumulative total, not per-call: `limitUsed + value > valueLimit`.
Cumulative token spend cap, lifetime — YES, chain-enforced, DEPLOYED on 56 (SpendingLimitsPolicy). Counts spend + outstanding approvals.
Cumulative spend cap over a ROLLING window — NO. Nothing ships this. Custom policy required.
Expiry — module EXISTS (TimeFramePolicy, validAfter/validUntil via _packValidationData so the EntryPoint honours it) but NOT DEPLOYED on 56. Deploy it.
Call-count cap — UsageLimitPolicy exists, NOT DEPLOYED on 56.
Instant revocation — chain-enforced via SmartSession session removal (an onchain tx). Caveat: "instant" is one block plus whatever is already in the bundler mempool; a UserOp already submitted may land first. For 7702 accounts, re-delegation is a stronger global kill switch.

interfaces.name: ERC-7715 — status and RPC surface
interfaces.body:
eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-7715

Status:   Draft
Category: Standards Track: ERC
Requires: ERC-7710 (hard dependency)

RPC method:  wallet_requestExecutionPermissions
  (NOT wallet_grantPermissions — older material uses the stale name)

Permission shape:
  BasePermission {
    type: string                 // identifier of the permission kind
    isAdjustmentAllowed: boolean // wallet may narrow/alter the request
    data: <type-specific fields>
  }

The EIP deliberately does NOT mandate an exhaustive permission-type list:
  "we expect more rule and permission types to be developed as wallets
   get more advanced"

Response MUST include a `delegationManager` address; redemption of the
granted permission goes through ERC-7710's interfaces and its permission-
context enforcement.

=> 7715 is a REQUEST/negotiation protocol. Enforcement strength is a
   property of the delegationManager contract, not of the standard.

gaps: BUNDLERS ON CHAIN 56 — NOT VERIFIED. My attempted fetch of docs.pimlico.io/references/supported-chains 404'd, and the fallback search returned only eco.com aggregator/marketing content with no primary confirmation. I have ZERO primary evidence that Pimlico, Alchemy, Biconomy, Stackup, Candide or Etherspot actually accept eth_sendUserOperation for chain 56. This is a hard blocker for any ERC-4337 design — verify by calling eth_supportedEntryPoints against each provider's chain-56 endpoint with a real API key before committing.
PAYMASTERS ON CHAIN 56 — NOT VERIFIED AT ALL. No addresses, no provider confirmation. If AiKi wants gasless agent execution on BSC this is unresearched.

BICONOMY (Nexus), SAFE (+ Safe7579 adapter), THIRDWEB, ALCHEMY (Modular Account / Account Kit) — none verified for chain 56. No addresses probed, no docs fetched. The task asked for all six SDKs; I only reached ZeroDev (docs listing only, chain 56 present) and Rhinestone (verified onchain). Treat the other four as unknown.

ZERODEV/KERNEL ON BSC IS DOCS-ONLY. docs.zerodev.app lists chain 56, but I did not eth_getCode a single Kernel implementation, factory, or ZeroDev permission-validator address on chain 56. The docs page also does not state which Kernel or EntryPoint version applies on 56.

ERC-6900 vs ERC-7579 TRACTION — NOT RESEARCHED. I have onchain proof that the 7579 SmartSession stack is deployed on BSC and zero data on 6900. That asymmetry is suggestive but is NOT a traction measurement. No ERC-6900 module addresses, no 6900 permission/session-key modules examined.

ERC-7710 SPEC TEXT NOT FETCHED. Everything I say about 7710 comes from ERC-7715's references to it (delegationManager, permission context redemption). I did not read the 7710 EIP, do not know its status (Draft/Review/Final), its DelegationManager interface, or whether any DelegationManager is deployed on BSC. MetaMask's Delegation Toolkit is the likely implementation and I did not verify it on chain 56.
NO WALLET SUPPORT DATA for 7715/7710. I cannot name a single wallet that implements wallet_requestExecutionPermissions in production, on BSC or anywhere.

AUDIT CONTENT UNREAD. I confirmed five audit PDFs exist in the smartsessions repo (including a 2026 Cantina report on external policies) but opened none. No severity counts, no findings, no remediation status. Do not represent SmartSessions as "audited clean" on my say-so.

SMARTSESSION ACTION ENCODING UNVERIFIED. I did not read contracts/DataTypes.sol, ISmartSession.sol, SmartSession.sol, UniActionPolicy.sol or ArgPolicy.sol. So the exact ActionId derivation (my belief: keccak over target+selector), the Session/PermissionId struct, the enable/disable/revoke function signatures, and the ArgPolicy rule encoding are all UNCONFIRMED. I deliberately state no function signatures for these rather than guess.

SMARTSESSION DEPLOYMENT PROVENANCE ON BSC. eth_getCode proves code exists at the module-sdk addresses on 56 and that SmartSession self-reports isModuleType(1)==true. I did NOT bytecode-diff against a canonical deployment on another chain (my Ethereum/Base public RPCs returned 403), and I did not check BscScan verification status. Before production use, verify the deployed bytecode matches the audited source.

THE 7702 DELEGATE IMPLEMENTATIONS ON BSC ARE UNIDENTIFIED. I have the most-used delegate addresses by auth count but could not attribute them to Kernel, Nexus, Safe, MetaMask, Binance Wallet, or anything else. Knowing which implementation dominates BSC 7702 traffic would materially change the integration choice.

NO BEP NUMBER FOR EIP-7702. The BNB Chain blog names EIP-7702 and separately names BEP-439 (EIP-2537), but I did not find a BEP document specifically covering the 7702 implementation on BSC, nor a BEP that documents BSC-specific 7702 deviations (if any exist).

PASTEUR HARDFORK LANDS 2026-08-25, one week out at time of writing. I did not research what it changes. If it touches 7702, 4337 gas accounting, or EIP-7623-style calldata pricing it could affect AiKi's assumptions.

BUNDLER STORAGE RULES vs CUSTOM POLICIES. A custom rolling-window policy must write storage during validation. ERC-7562 / bundler validation rules restrict which storage a validation phase may touch. I did not verify whether an associated-storage write in a policy module is accepted by the bundlers serving BSC — this could silently break the exact feature AiKi most wants.
aiki_implications: THE HONEST SENTENCE AiKi CAN SHIP TODAY, chain-enforced end to end: "This agent may call <target> with at most 250 USDT total. You can revoke it in one transaction." Every clause there is enforced by deployed bytecode on chain 56. Do NOT append "per 30 days" unless you deploy a custom policy — see below.

THE 30-DAY CLAUSE HAS TWO HONEST FORMS. (a) NON-RENEWING, available now: cap = 250 USDT lifetime (SpendingLimitsPolicy, deployed on 56) + session expiry at now+30d (TimeFramePolicy — you must deploy it, it is NOT on 56). This gives literally "at most 250 USDT over the next 30 days" and is fully chain-enforced. This is almost certainly what your users actually want and it needs no new Solidity. (b) RENEWING ("250 every 30 days"): nothing ships this. Requires a custom IActionPolicy. Do not describe (a) as (b) in the UI.

DEPLOY-FIRST TASK LIST for BSC, in order: (1) CREATE2-deploy TimeFramePolicy, ValueLimitPolicy and UsageLimitPolicy from the audited erc7579/smartsessions source to their canonical addresses on 56 — they are missing and they are permissionless deploys, so you get the same addresses as every other chain and stay SDK-compatible. This is a half-day of work that removes your single biggest capability gap. (2) Verify all of them on BscScan. (3) Only then consider a custom rolling-window policy.

PREFER EIP-7702 OVER FRESH 4337 ACCOUNTS on BSC. 7702 is live (1.4% of all BSC txs), lets a user's EXISTING BSC EOA gain 7579 module support without changing address or migrating funds, and gives you a nuclear revoke that a plain 7579 account does not have: re-signing an authorization to a different implementation invalidates every installed module's authority at once, in one EOA-signed tx, with replay protection from the auth nonce. For an agent-commerce trust product, "one signature kills everything" is a headline safety feature.

ARCHITECTURAL TRAP — WHERE THE SPEND CAP ACTUALLY BINDS. ERC20SpendingLimitPolicy is ERC-20-calldata-aware: it decodes approve/transfer/transferFrom and counts approvals against the cap. Venus.repayBorrow pulls funds via transferFrom, so the cap must be installed on the USDT TOKEN as the action target, not on Venus. If you install it against Venus you will cap nothing. Conversely, the target/selector allowlist ("may call Venus.repayBorrow") is a separate policy on the Venus target. You need BOTH, and they are different modules. Budget engineering time for getting this pairing right — it is the most likely source of a shipped-but-unenforced permission.

REVOCATION IS NOT INSTANT AND YOU SHOULD SAY SO. Revocation is an onchain state write: one BSC block (~0.75s post-Maxwell, but do not quote a number you have not measured) plus mempool. A UserOp already in a bundler's mempool can still land after the user hits revoke. "Revocable instantly" overstates it; "revocable in one transaction, effective within a block" is defensible. If you need a true instant kill, the 7702 re-delegation path is the strongest lever, and even that is one block.

BUNDLER DEPENDENCY IS YOUR RISK, NOT YOUR ENFORCEMENT. Enforcement is 100% onchain; a malicious bundler cannot make a session exceed its cap. But a bundler that refuses to relay is a liveness failure for the agent. Since I could not confirm ANY bundler serving chain 56, resolve that before design freeze — and note that with EIP-7702 you have a fallback: an agent can send a plain type-2 tx to the 7702-delegated account and bypass the 4337 mempool entirely, paying its own gas. Design so 4337 is an optimisation, not a hard dependency.

DO NOT BUILD ON ERC-7715 YET. It is Draft, the method name already changed to wallet_requestExecutionPermissions, the permission-type taxonomy is explicitly open-ended, and enforcement is delegated to an unspecified delegationManager contract. A 7715 grant is not a security guarantee. If you adopt it, adopt it as an optional REQUEST surface layered on top of your SmartSession enforcement, and always resolve the actual constraint by reading the policy contract state onchain — never by trusting the grant JSON.

AiKi's DIFFERENTIATOR IS THE VERIFIABILITY UI, AND IT IS BUILDABLE. Every constraint above is readable from chain state: SpendingLimitsPolicy exposes a getter returning (spendingLimit, alreadySpent, approvedAmount). You can render a live, chain-sourced "237.50 of 250 USDT remaining, enforced by contract 0x00000088D4…6343" with a BscScan link. That is a category-defining trust feature and it costs you one eth_call. Ship it.

DRAW A HARD LINE IN THE PRODUCT: never let a backend-enforced limit render with the same visual language as a chain-enforced one. If any AiKi flow uses a co-signer, simulate-then-sign, or backend rate limiting, its UI string must be "AiKi will not permit" and never "the chain will not permit". Given AiKi is selling trust in agent execution, conflating the two once is an existential credibility risk — and, per the finding above, you do not need to conflate them, because the chain-enforced path genuinely works on BSC today.
